revise.summary: I revised content/lessons/09-implement.md, and both gates pass: the lint prints no ERROR lines at 2,902 words, and vitest ran 13 tests with all passing. The illustrative chat Scene now follows code-review as 1.3.1 runs it. It asks for a fixed point, finds an empty diff because nothing is committed yet, the run commits, and you then type /mattpocock-skills:code-review main yourself. The Try it steps, the rough-edges paragraph and the Cheat sheet now give the same workaround. The Site story now uses only repo facts: the PR #9 body and commits, the ticket files, the spec, and the old journal at d21fc2c. I cut the claims only a session log could back (/workflows, "13 findings", "three problems", "asked it to go faster", "called by its full name") and replaced the 13 with the journal's "about 15". It now says the PR exists because the author's first message asked for one. Quiz changes: scenario-whole-spec became predict-frontier, so goal 3 is now tested. Checkpoint next-ticket became two-terminals, which tests the one-checkout rule instead of repeating spot-no-clear. I also rewrote the loop-choice prompt, the serial-harness options and the mid-run-review prompt, and replaced several distractors. I checked every Matt claim against the cached transcripts and the two community claims against their pages. Matt's manual loop is now "not really workable", the "no infrastructure, watch and steer" point is credited to the docs, and the 100k figure is the room he had left in that session, not a rule for every job. I also added the definitions a cold reader was missing.

quiz.where: Goals, line 15 ("choose between `/implement` in the same window, `/implement` once per ticket with `/clear` between, and `/implement-spec`"); Final test as a whole (lines 312-430)
quiz.problem: Goal 2 is a three-way choice, but no Final test question has `/implement-spec` as the right pick. It is a wrong option in scenario-plan-in-chat (line 320), scenario-serial-harness (line 338) and scenario-loop-choice (line 364). predict-frontier, spot-midrun-review and predict-run-end all assume the run has already started. A reader who thinks "never pick `/implement-spec`" scores full marks. Meanwhile the `/clear`-between-tickets branch is tested twice: scenario-serial-harness's right answer (line 344) and spot-no-clear's right answer (line 386), and serial-harness's option b (line 340) is spot-no-clear's scenario.
quiz.evidence: Writing guide, Questions: "Every goal gets at least one Final test question." ask-matt SKILL.md:27 gives the decision rule the Lesson teaches at line 129: reach for `/implement-spec` "when you'd rather orchestrate the build than drive each ticket yourself". docs/engineering/implement-spec.md:13 and :22 give the other conditions (tickets with blocking edges; a harness that runs background sub-agents in worktrees). The Lesson is a new Slug (`git show main:content/lessons/` has no 09-implement.md), so no question ids are published yet.
quiz.fix:
Replace spot-no-clear with a judgement question where `/implement-spec` is right. That still leaves 5 scenario-, 2 spot- and 1 sequence- ids. Put the right answer first to keep the a/b/c/d spread:

```test scenario-pick-spec-run
Your book-club spec has eight tickets from `/to-tickets`, and once the first lands, four of them can start. Claude Code on your laptop can run several helpers at once, each in its own copy of the project. You'd rather not start each ticket yourself, and checking one finished branch at the end suits you. In a cleared session, what do you type?
- [x] `/implement-spec`, pointing it at the spec's file
  > Right. It reads the blocking edges as a graph, starts the four ready tickets at once in their own worktrees, and lands everything on one integration branch for one review.
- [ ] `/implement` with all eight ticket files, so one run builds them all
  > One run takes one ticket. Eight in one window head straight for the dumb zone.
- [ ] `/implement` on the first ticket, then `/clear` and the next, by hand
  > That works, but it makes you the dispatcher, the job you wanted to hand off.
- [ ] `/tdd` once per ticket, then `/mattpocock-skills:code-review` at the end
  > `/tdd` builds one behaviour test-first. It doesn't read tickets or their blocking edges, so you'd still be the dispatcher.
```

quiz.where: Final test, `test spot-no-clear`, prompt line 385 ("By ticket 4 the agent forgot names it had agreed and its review missed obvious problems") and option b, line 388
quiz.problem: The symptoms argue against the intended answer. If names were agreed in the conversation, `/clear` would erase them completely, so "forgot names it had agreed" points to "write the names down", which is what distractor b offers ("run `/to-spec` again"). "Its review missed obvious problems" fits badly with line 44, which says code-review runs each axis in a sub-agent with a fresh, empty memory. A sharp reader can argue a full parent window doesn't explain the reviewers missing things. Two options become arguable.
quiz.evidence: Lesson line 82: each ticket "fits one fresh context window and carries what it needs". ask-matt SKILL.md:26: "Each ticket is self-contained, so the last one's context is disposable." code-review SKILL.md:11: both axes run "as parallel sub-agents so they don't pollute each other's context". Lesson line 44: "a helper with a fresh, empty memory".
quiz.fix: If spot-no-clear is kept rather than replaced (previous finding), make the symptoms point only at a filling window. Replace the prompt with: "Ana worked through four tickets with `/implement`, one after another in a single session. Tickets 1 and 2 came out clean. By ticket 4 the agent was skipping details written in the ticket itself and making slips it hadn't made on ticket 1. Spot the mistake." Replace option b's feedback with: "The spec and tickets already hold the plan. Rewriting them doesn't free up the window."

quiz.where: Final test, `test scenario-afk-task`, lines 348-358 (right option line 352: "A well-specified ticket with agreed seams, in a sandbox.")
quiz.problem: Weak distractors plus a wording tell. The right option is the only ticket and the only option carrying the Lesson's safety words (well-specified, agreed seams, sandbox). The three distractors are a grilling session, a one-way change to the live production database, and an unseen layout choice. Each maps one-to-one onto line 186's list ("ambiguous, irreversible or hard to review afterwards"), so the question tests recognition of that sentence, not judgement. None of the distractors is tempting.
quiz.evidence: Lesson line 186: "It suits work that's ambiguous, irreversible or hard to review afterwards." Line 187 lists the AFK conditions: settle the ambiguity before, let tests and review stand in during, end with something reviewable. Writing guide: "Distractors are real misconceptions... no wording tells."
quiz.fix:
Make every option a ticket that breaks exactly one AFK condition, so the reader has to apply line 187:

```test scenario-afk-task
It's Friday evening. Which of these would you leave running AFK overnight?
- [ ] A ticket, in a sandbox, whose spec hasn't settled whether names are required.
  > That's an open question. Left alone, the agent fills it with a guess and builds tidy work on top of it.
- [x] A well-specified ticket with agreed seams, in a sandbox.
  > Right. The questions are settled before you leave, tests and review stand in for you, and the sandbox keeps your machine safe. It ends on a branch you check in the morning.
- [ ] A well-specified ticket whose only check is you clicking through the page.
  > If only you can verify it, nothing stands in for you overnight. Do it while you're there.
- [ ] A well-specified ticket that deletes old rows from the live database.
  > Irreversible work that touches production is exactly what to keep human-in-the-loop.
```

quiz.where: Checkpoint `run-once-first`, right option line 201 ("Run one pass by hand and watch what the agent does.") and stem line 200 ("What should you do first?")
quiz.problem: Wording tell. The right option repeats the section's highlighted phrase, and the stem's "first" completes it. A reader can match the words without understanding why a watched pass matters. It is also the shortest option.
quiz.evidence: Lesson line 197: "Whichever loop you build, ==run one pass by hand first==." Writing guide: "Don't restate the defining phrase of the right answer in the prompt" and "no wording tells".
quiz.fix: Reword the right option so it doesn't echo the highlight: "- [x] Start it on just one ticket and stay at the keyboard to watch." Keep the feedback: "Right. That's how Matt starts: one watched pass shows what to tune in the prompt before nobody is watching."

quiz.where: Checkpoint `shared-file`, right option line 180 ("Add a blocking edge between them, or have the exploration notes fix the exact label names.")
quiz.problem: The right option restates the body's own sentence from 13 lines earlier, nearly word for word. It also stands out as the most specific option. The Checkpoint tests recall of line 167, not whether the reader understands the fix.
quiz.evidence: Lesson line 167: "Add a blocking edge, or have the exploration notes fix the names." Writing guide: "Questions test transfer, not recognition" and "no wording tells".
quiz.fix: "- [x] Make one wait for the other, or agree the label names before the run." Feedback: "Right. A blocking edge runs them one after the other, and agreed names, carried in the exploration notes, mean both start from the same words. Ask for either when you start the run."

quiz.where: Final test, `test spot-on-main`, prompt line 373 ("Sam opened Claude Code in the project, which was on `main`, typed `/implement` with the ticket, and now the commit is on `main`.")
quiz.problem: The prompt states the cause. It says Sam wanted a branch, the project was on `main`, and the commit is on `main`. The reader only has to join two sentences, so there is nothing left to spot.
quiz.evidence: Right option, line 374: "Sam didn't create and switch to a branch before typing `/implement`." Writing guide: "Don't restate the defining phrase of the right answer in the prompt."
quiz.fix: Drop the clause that names the starting branch: "Sam wanted the new search feature on its own branch, ready for a pull request. Sam opened Claude Code in the project, typed `/implement` with the ticket, and the run went well. Afterwards, the new commit is on `main`. Spot the mistake."

quiz.where: Final test, spot- questions: options at lines 376, 378 ("Sam should have…"), 388, 392 ("She should have…"), 402 ("Jo should have…"); right options at lines 374, 386, 400
quiz.problem: Phrasing tell across questions. All five options that start "X should have…" are wrong. Every right option is a plain past-tense account of what happened ("Sam didn't create…", "She never typed…", "The review ran while…"). A test-wise reader can drop every "should have" option in all three spot questions without reading them.
quiz.evidence: Lesson lines 374-404 as quoted. Lens rule: "do the wrong options share a phrasing the right one lacks".
quiz.fix: Write every option in the same past-tense form. spot-on-main b: "Sam didn't run `/mattpocock-skills:code-review` before typing `/implement`." spot-on-main c: "Sam didn't type `/clear` before `/implement`, so no clean branch was made." spot-midrun-review c: "Jo reviewed everything at once instead of one worktree at a time." If spot-no-clear stays: b "She didn't run `/to-spec` again between tickets." and d "She didn't open a pull request after every single ticket."

quiz.where: Final test, `test sequence-one-run`, option a line 410 ("Commit → fetch the ticket → tdd slices → full suite → code-review")
quiz.problem: The distractor is a throwaway: no reader commits before fetching the work, and the feedback admits as much ("At the start, nothing is built yet"). That leaves effectively three options. A tempting slip is review before the full suite.
quiz.evidence: implement SKILL.md:13 ("the full test suite once at the end") and :15 ("Once done, call the Skill tool with "code-review"").
quiz.fix: "- [ ] Fetch the ticket → tdd slices → code-review → full suite → commit" with feedback "  > The full suite runs once when the build is finished, and the review checks that finished work after it."

quiz.where: Final test, `test scenario-plan-in-chat`, prompt line 313 ("Nothing was written to a file") and option b feedback line 317
quiz.problem: "Nothing was written to a file" mirrors the reason behind the right answer (line 80: "The plan is in this conversation, not a file"), so it hints at option c. Option b can also be argued: the Lesson's own Try it (step 5) puts the plan inside the `/implement` message itself, and b's feedback ("Clearing throws away the decisions") ignores that b re-describes them.
quiz.fix: Prompt: "You've just grilled a small change to a recipe site with the agent: a 'print this recipe' button. The session has plenty of room left. What do you type?" Option b feedback: "With plenty of room left, clearing gains nothing and throws away the grilling's detail. A rewritten description rarely carries every decision."

quiz.where: Checkpoint `ticket-still-open`, prompt line 56 and right option line 59 ("Check the work, then close the ticket and tick its boxes yourself.")
quiz.problem: The prompt ("still says 'ready-for-agent' and none of its boxes are ticked") and the right option repeat line 49's parenthetical. The Checkpoint checks recall of that sentence rather than the idea that the run ends at the commit.
quiz.evidence: Lesson line 49: "or close the ticket (on a local tracker, change its status from "ready-for-agent" and tick its checklist boxes). Those jobs are yours."
quiz.fix: Right option: "- [x] Check the work, then mark the ticket done yourself." Keep the feedback.

quiz.where: Final test, `test spot-midrun-review`, option d line 404 ("A code review can't run on an integration branch.")
quiz.problem: The distractor is obviously silly. The Lesson says plainly that `/implement-spec` runs its review on the integration branch (line 140), and the option's own feedback says so.
quiz.evidence: Lesson line 140: "does it call code-review, once, over the whole branch"; implement-spec SKILL.md:36 ("call the Skill tool with `code-review` on the integration branch").
quiz.fix: "- [ ] Jo's spec had too many tickets for one `/implement-spec` run." with feedback "  > Nothing in the Skill caps the ticket count. Six is a normal run. The timing of the review was the problem."

reader.where: Try it yourself, step 3: "If Node.js isn't installed, use Python with pytest and mypy instead." (line 248; prerequisites line 228)
reader.problem: Step 3 needs Node.js or Python, but the Try it never lists either as a prerequisite, and the course tells readers they don't need Node. A Windows Visitor set up the way Start here says has Claude Code (native installer) and Git for Windows, and neither one brings Node.js or Python. On that machine the prompt's only fallback fails too, so building the project depends on the agent making something up.
reader.evidence: content/lessons/00-start-here.md:36 says "Node.js is optional. Claude Code doesn't need this JavaScript tool." content/lessons/00-start-here.md:35 lists only Git for Windows for Windows users. content/lessons/09-implement.md:228 asks only for Claude Code and Git. In comparison, content/lessons/13-diagnosing-bugs.md:239 does cover the no-runtime case ("in Node or Python if either is installed here, otherwise in bash").
reader.fix: Line 228: "You need Claude Code installed and signed in (see [Start here](/learn/start-here)), Git, and Node.js or Python. If `git --version` says it isn't found, install Git first. If neither `node --version` nor `python --version` (`python3 --version` on a Mac) prints a version, install Node.js (the LTS installer from nodejs.org) and open a new terminal." Step 3 prompt: "...and one test for it. Use Node.js if it's installed, otherwise Python with pytest and mypy. If neither is installed, stop and tell me. Commit it on main."

reader.where: Try it yourself, step 3: "Commit it on main." (line 248)
reader.problem: A fresh Git install has no user.name or user.email. Common on Windows, the first commit then stops with "Author identity unknown / Please tell me who you are". The Lesson says nothing about this, so a Visitor who barely knows Git hits an error they can't read on the very first commit. Other Lessons in the course handle this case and this one doesn't.
reader.evidence: content/lessons/06-prototype.md:235: "If Git says \"Please tell me who you are\", run the two `git config --global` lines it shows...". content/lessons/13-diagnosing-bugs.md:239: "(if Git has no name and email, set placeholder ones for this folder)". Running grep -n "user.name\|git config" on content/lessons/00-start-here.md and 09-implement.md finds nothing.
reader.fix: Step 3 prompt: "...and one test for it. If Git has no name and email yet, set placeholder ones for this folder only. Commit it on main."

reader.where: Try it yourself, step 2: "Type a slash and the word implement. If `implement` isn't in the list that pops up, type `/exit`..." (line 239)
reader.problem: The step leaves `/implement` sitting in the input box and never says not to press Enter, or to delete it before step 3. A beginner who presses Enter starts `/implement` with no plan in an empty repo. Step 3's setup prompt then lands in the middle of a running Skill.
reader.evidence: Lesson line 239. Step 3 (line 245) expects a clean prompt. The implement SKILL.md:7 ("Implement the work described by the user in the spec or tickets") would start looking for a spec that doesn't exist.
reader.fix: "Type a slash and the word implement, but don't press Enter. If `implement` shows in the list that pops up, delete what you typed and go on to step 3. If it isn't there, delete it, type `/exit`, install Matt's Skills, then run `claude` again:"

reader.where: A session, step by step, Scene caption: "The review only reads committed work, and nothing is committed yet, so it finds nothing." (line 116), against How Matt and others use it: "There, `/implement` ran code-review's two axes in sub-agents, then committed" (line 216)
reader.problem: The Lesson contradicts itself. The Scene says the review inside the run always sees nothing because the commit comes after it. A few sections later, Matt's real `/implement` run reviews on both axes before committing. The real condition is whether the branch already has commits since the fixed point, and a cold reader is never told that.
reader.evidence: code-review SKILL.md:21-23 (~/.claude/plugins/cache/claude-plugins-official/mattpocock-skills/1.3.1/skills/engineering/code-review/SKILL.md) diffs `git diff <fixed-point>...HEAD` (committed work only) and fails when the diff is empty. implement SKILL.md:15-17 reviews and then commits. Research note .scratch/course-rewrite/research/implement.md:103 records that Matt's review ran with two sub-agents and then committed.
reader.fix: Line 116 caption: "# The review reads only what's been committed since the fixed point. This new branch has no commits yet, so it finds nothing. Then it commits and stops. The ticket stays open."

reader.where: Building a whole spec, flow Scene "The five tickets behind this site's redesign", last caption: "All five tickets are in, so code-review runs over the whole branch..." (line 160), against the Site story: "An early review still ran while 05 was building." (line 297)

reader.evidence: git show d21fc2c:content/lessons/11-main-flow.md, item 5: "An early review ran while 05 was still being built." .scratch/main-flow-and-redesign/issues/04-main-flow-lesson.md:27 records the author asking "do I run the code review now or after?".
reader.fix: Last caption: "# All five tickets are in. The Skill's one review runs here, over the whole branch, and one fix-up agent fixes every finding. (On this run an early review had also started while 05 was building; the Site story tells how.)"

reader.where: Final test spot-no-clear: "Ana worked through four tickets with `/implement`, one after another in a single session." (line 385)
reader.problem: The stem gives away the answer: "in a single session" just means "never cleared". One distractor is also weak: "She worked the tickets in order instead of all at once" is plainly wrong to anyone who read the Lesson. The question tests recognition, not transfer.
reader.evidence: Lesson line 385, and the right option at line 386: "She never typed `/clear` between one ticket and the next." Writing guide, pilot lessons: "Don't restate the defining phrase of the right answer in the prompt."
reader.fix: Stem: "Ana worked through four tickets with `/implement` one afternoon. Tickets 1 and 2 came out clean. By ticket 4 the agent forgot names it had agreed and its review missed obvious problems. Spot the mistake." Replace the third option with "She should have run code-review herself after each ticket.", feedback: "`/implement` already reviews each ticket. The review was weak because the window was full."

reader.where: The idea: one run of `/implement`: "So when `/to-tickets` finishes, nothing starts building by itself" (line 36)

reader.evidence: Line 36 is the first mention. Line 82: "`/to-tickets` (which splits it into tickets; see [Spec + tickets](/learn/spec-and-issues))".
reader.fix: "So when `/to-tickets` (the Skill that splits a spec into tickets) finishes, nothing starts building by itself: typing `/implement` is your move."

reader.where: A session, step by step: "after the commit, type the Skill's full name, plugin first." (line 125)

reader.fix: "...plus a short list of classic code smells, common signs of code that will be hard to change?"

reader.where: How Matt and others use it: "He put his own Smart zone at about 140k tokens then, leaving roughly 100k of room for the job" (line 215)
